clue.text: & 4, 21 Alarming Epstein files involved arrangements of adults with children

indicators.note: people who are involved are tangled up with one another, and tangled letters keep none of the order they came in

parts.note: twenty letters, the whole phrase redealt across three entries

explanation.surface: Released Epstein files turn out to describe, alarmingly, how adults were paired up with children.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole tail of the clue and does the misdirection by itself: a phrase that sounds like the scandal and means the ordinary household. The answer runs 1, 4, then 21.
explanation.definitionFit: Single-parent families are homes where one adult is raising the children, which is one very common arrangement of adults with children.

clue.text: Resilience shown by American going after male in disgrace

indicators.note: the American's letter comes after the rest
one piece set in another goes inside it

parts.note: a stain is a mark of disgrace

explanation.surface: An American shows grit in pursuing a disgraced man.
explanation.definitionFit: Stamina is staying power, the ability to endure and keep going, which is resilience.

clue.text: Fingers celebs

definitions.meaning: to finger someone is to point them out, the informer's job
the big ones are the famous people themselves

explanation.surface: An informer points out which celebrities were in on it.
explanation.walkthrough: A two-word clue is nearly always two definitions, because there is no room for anything else. One half wants a verb and the other a plural noun, and the same five letters serve both.
explanation.definitionFit: To name someone is to finger them to the authorities, and a big name is a celebrity, so both halves are everyday uses of the one word.

clue.text: Dog with lead on biting children, right?

indicators.note: to bite into something is to close your teeth round it, so the biting word shuts on both sides of what it takes

parts.note: to lead someone on is to lure them
ch = children, as on a price list
r = right

explanation.surface: A dog held on its lead is snapping at passing children.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lead' is the leash in the surface and the verb to entice in the wordplay, which is where the whole four-letter chunk comes from. A lurcher is a greyhound crossed with a working dog, long the poacher's dog in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: A lurcher is a crossbred sighthound kept for hunting rabbits and hares, so 'dog' names it by kind.

clue.text: see 1ac.
Topless bar with US-style jugs for strong drink

indicators.note: a topless word has lost its top, which in a down clue is its first letter

parts.note: taken as written, before it loses its first letter
rack is American slang for a woman's breasts, which British slang calls jugs

explanation.surface: A topless bar in the American style serves strong drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Topless' strips the B from BAR to leave AR. Jugs is British slang for breasts, and rack is the American equivalent. Arrack is a spirit distilled in South and Southeast Asia.
explanation.definitionFit: Arrack is a potent spirit distilled from palm sap, rice or sugar cane, so a strong alcoholic drink.

clue.text: Sexy rogue one's screwing

indicators.note: a screw turns as it goes in, and letters given a turn come out in a different order

parts.note: nine letters, the apostrophe ignored as always

explanation.surface: The attractive scoundrel somebody is currently sleeping with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One's' looks like idle grammar and hands over four of the nine letters. 'Sexy' stands alone at the front, which leaves every other word in the clue doing wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: An erogenous zone is one that responds to sexual touch, so the adjective means sexually charged rather than good-looking.

clue.text: Sink party after misguided trope

indicators.note: after puts the party letters at the end, following the rearranged word
something misguided has gone astray, so the letters of trope are put in a wrong order

parts.note: taken as written, as the letters to rearrange
a do is a party or celebration

explanation.surface: A political party sinks after relying on a misjudged figure of speech.
explanation.walkthrough: 'misguided' rearranges TROPE into TORPE, and 'after' puts DO behind it.
explanation.definitionFit: To torpedo something is to wreck or scupper it, just as the weapon sinks a ship.

clue.text: Prince in group with sex instigated by bloke with boat — fair play

indicators.note: to instigate something is to start it off, so what is wanted is the letter the word starts on

parts.note: a sort is a kind or group of things

indicators.note: a prince put in a word is surrounded by it, that word opening to take him

parts.note: p = prince
the first letter of Sex, the one instigating it asks for
a bloke is a man
a ship is a boat to everyone except a sailor

explanation.surface: A prince joins a group for sex, egged on by a bloke who has a boat.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points straight at the Epstein story, which is what makes the definition land where it does. 'Instigated' looks like a whole man's doing and asks only for one letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Sportsmanship is playing by the rules and taking the result without complaint, which is fair play under another name.

clue.text: Royal home — ousted royal, abject, low, starts missing comfort

indicators.note: the start of a word is the letter it opens on, one from each word listed

parts.note: Balmoral, the monarch's castle in Aberdeenshire and the family's summer house

indicators.note: what is missing has gone from the word it sat in, and the rest closes up

parts.note: the letters Ousted, Royal, Abject and Low start on, which the castle then loses from its end

explanation.surface: A royal turned out of the family home, brought low and badly in need of consolation.
explanation.walkthrough: Four words in a row give up their first letters, and the string they spell is the part to throw away rather than keep. 'Royal' earns its keep twice, once in each half of the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A balm soothes a wound or a mood, so the noun stands for comfort itself rather than for anything that provides it.

clue.text: Range of skills of i.e. reporter rubbished

indicators.note: to rubbish something is to tear it apart, and torn-up letters go back together any way at all

parts.note: ten letters, the full stops dropped

explanation.surface: A reporter's abilities are being publicly rubbished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I.e.' earns nothing in the sentence, and a word that contributes nothing to the surface is usually contributing letters. Here it lends the first two of the ten.
explanation.definitionFit: A repertoire is the stock of pieces or tricks a performer can call on at will, which is a range of skills.

clue.text: Keir's heading off shit going round college — "Trash!"

indicators.note: the heading of a word is its first letter

parts.note: its first letter is K

indicators.note: the scrambled letters go round the letter for college
off means gone bad, so the letters of the rude word are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written, as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Keir Starmer storms off, telling the rubbish surrounding his college to clear out.
explanation.walkthrough: K comes from 'Keir's heading'; 'off' rearranges SHIT into ITSH, and 'going round' wraps it about C to give ITSCH.
explanation.definitionFit: Kitsch is tasteless, garish art or decoration, the sort of thing scornfully called trash.

clue.text: Took off dress and celebrated pulling females

indicators.note: and puts the two shortened words side by side
pulling here means pulling out, so the letters for females are removed

parts.note: a frock is a dress
F is the abbreviation for female; the plural gives two, one from each word
feted means celebrated or honoured

explanation.surface: Someone stripped off a dress and partied after picking up women.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pulling' takes the F (female) out of FROCK and the other F out of FETED, leaving ROCK and ETED. 'Took off' looks like undressing but means soared.
explanation.definitionFit: To rocket is to shoot up fast like a launched missile, so it means the same as took off.

clue.text: Bum spots first signs of panicky president blocking vote — over-hasty

indicators.note: the first sign of a word is the letter it opens with, one taken from each
something blocking a word is stuck in the middle of it, the word parting to make room

parts.note: a nay is a vote against, the one recorded opposite aye
the first letters of Panicky and President
a rash decision is an over-hasty one

explanation.surface: A panicking president is blocking the vote and being reckless about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bum spots' sits at the front doing the defining while everything after it paints a political scene. A nay is the vote recorded against, which is the only sense that gives up letters here.
explanation.definitionFit: Nappy rash is the red soreness a baby gets under its nappy, and under the nappy is exactly where the bum is.

clue.text: Leader there around island with duke

indicators.note: what goes around a thing closes on both sides of it

parts.note: someone there is present
i = island, as marked on charts
d = duke

explanation.surface: A leader tours an island in the company of a duke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'There' looks like the least useful word in the sentence and is the seven-letter chunk everything else fits into. The island and the duke are one letter each, dropped in side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: A president heads a republic, a company or a club, so 'leader' is the bare job description.

clue.text: Start to crap in toilet (potty)

indicators.note: the start of a word is the letter it opens on

parts.note: the loo is the British toilet

indicators.note: a letter put in a word goes inside it, the word splitting round it

parts.note: the first letter of Crap

explanation.surface: Somebody settling down to a crap in the toilet.
explanation.walkthrough: The brackets make 'potty' look like an aside about the lavatory when it is the definition, meaning mad. Loco came into English from Spanish, where it means exactly that.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone loco is out of their mind, which is what potty means in British English.

clue.text: Police coming back to arrest husband and other people

indicators.note: arresting a suspect means holding that person in custody, so the husband's letter goes inside
coming back means returning, so the word for the police is read backwards

parts.note: the Met is London's Metropolitan Police

explanation.surface: Officers return to arrest a husband and others involved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming back' reverses MET to TEM, and 'to arrest' holds H inside it. The Met is London's Metropolitan Police.
explanation.definitionFit: Them is the pronoun for people other than the speaker and listener, those others.

clue.text: One you can't trust with property and gold

parts.note: a property in the sense of a characteristic is a trait
or = gold in heraldry, the tincture named on a shield

explanation.surface: A man who can be left alone with neither your possessions nor your gold.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Property' is possessions in the surface and a quality in the wordplay, the sense in 'the properties of a metal'. Heraldry's or for gold is worth learning early, because setters never signal it.
explanation.definitionFit: A traitor betrays the side that trusted them, so 'one you can't trust' is the warning given about them.

clue.text: Send email that's rehashed euphemism for predatory males?

definitions.note: The definition does not give a synonym but names what the answer is: the polite phrase such men get described by.

indicators.note: a rehash serves the same material up in a new form, and letters served up again need not keep their places

parts.note: nine letters, the message and the instruction to send it

explanation.surface: An old email is reworded and sent out again.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the definition as a euphemism, a phrase that sounds courtly and is used to cover for men who are nothing of the kind. Everything before 'that's' is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A ladies' man is flattered as charming with women, which is the soft label the clue says is covering for something worse.

clue.text: Frantically question having ball amputated for examination

indicators.note: acting frantically means in a wild disorder, so the remaining letters are jumbled
having begins 'having ball amputated': something is to be cut away from the word
amputated means cut off, so the ball letter is removed from the word

parts.note: taken as written, the word that is cut down
O is round like a ball

explanation.surface: A patient frantically asks about having a testicle removed during a medical examination.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having ball amputated' takes O out of QUESTION to leave QUESTIN, and 'Frantically' rearranges it. 'ball' and 'amputated' paint surgery, but the ball is just the letter O.
explanation.definitionFit: An inquest is an official judicial inquiry into the facts of a case, especially a death, so a formal examination.

clue.text: Predator primarily involved with teen is a predator no more

indicators.note: involved means tangled up, so these letters are rearranged
primarily means first of all, so take the first letter

explanation.surface: A predator who got involved with a teenager is dead and preys no more.
explanation.walkthrough: Jeffrey Epstein was an American financier and convicted sex offender who died in jail in 2019.
explanation.definitionFit: Epstein preyed on underage girls; having died, he is a former abuser who can harm nobody now.

clue.text: Order cocaine from idiot — twat dismissive of women

indicators.note: taking one thing from another leaves the other short by exactly that much
to dismiss something is to send it away, so that letter leaves the word it was in

parts.note: a dick is an idiot
c = cocaine, the letter taken out of the idiot
the four letters as they stand, before the cut
w = women, the letter dismissed from the word before it

explanation.surface: Scoring cocaine off an idiot, a twat with no time for women.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are built the same way, a crude word for a person minus the letter another word names. 'Order' at the front is the noun, the decree, not the verb the surface wants.
explanation.definitionFit: A diktat is an order handed down and not up for discussion, the sort nobody is invited to vote on.

clue.text: see 1 ac
Sick question you texted: "Sexually available?"

indicators.note: a word texted is spelt the short way, by the single letter that sounds like it

parts.note: q = question
u = you, the way a phone spells it
someone called easy is being described as sexually available

explanation.surface: A text message puts a blunt question about how available somebody is.
explanation.walkthrough: The colon and the quotation marks dress the last two words up as the message being sent, when they are the last four letters. 'Sick' is the nauseous sense, not the slang one.
explanation.definitionFit: To feel queasy is to feel sick in the stomach, the turning feeling rather than any actual illness.

clue.text: Contact 19's top guy on the phone

indicators.note: in a down clue, the top of a word is its first letter

parts.note: 19 down is EPSTEIN, so this refers to that word

indicators.note: words heard on the phone are sounded, not seen, so the word for guy is entered as its soundalike

parts.note: a guy is a male

explanation.surface: Getting in touch with Epstein's most senior man by telephone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'top' takes E from 19 down; 'on the phone' changes MALE into the identical-sounding MAIL.
explanation.definitionFit: To email someone is to contact them by sending an electronic message.

clue.text: Experienced "bastard" setter is in Private Eye

indicators.note: bastard as an adjective means corrupt or not genuine, so the letters of setter are corrupted into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, as the letters to rearrange

indicators.note: the word is goes inside the next piece

parts.note: Private Eye refers to itself as we, the magazine's editorial voice

explanation.surface: A seasoned, nasty compiler works for the satirical magazine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bastard' rearranges SETTER into STREET, and 'in' puts IS inside WE to give WISE. Private Eye is a British satirical magazine, which this puzzle appears in.
explanation.definitionFit: Being streetwise means having the shrewd, worldly know-how that comes from experience of urban life.

clue.text: Means to pay a married old lover

parts.note: the article taken off the page as the letter it is
m = married, as on a form
an ex is an old flame

explanation.surface: Finding a way to pay off a married former lover.
explanation.walkthrough: Amex is the everyday short form of American Express, the charge card. The 'a' earns a letter of its own, which is easy to miss while it is posing as plain grammar.
explanation.definitionFit: An Amex is an American Express card, so producing one at the till is a means to pay.

clue.text: Spin (or backtracking?) by misogynist

indicators.note: by means next to, so the two pieces sit side by side
backtracking means going back the way one came, so the word or runs backwards

parts.note: Andrew Tate is a notorious online misogynist

explanation.surface: A notorious misogynist's media spin, or is he backtracking?
explanation.walkthrough: 'backtracking' turns OR into RO, and 'by' sets TATE beside it. Andrew Tate is an influencer known for misogynist views.
explanation.definitionFit: To rotate is to turn about an axis, which is to spin.

clue.text: "Lost out!" — Ghislaine, when finally nicked

indicators.note: out means not in its usual state, so the letters of lost are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, as the letters to rearrange

indicators.note: finally picks the final letter of each word

parts.note: the last letters of these two words are E and N

explanation.surface: Ghislaine Maxwell, exclaiming that she has lost, when finally arrested by the police.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges LOST into STOL, and 'finally' adds the last letters of Ghislaine and when. 'nicked' looks like arrested, but it means stolen.
explanation.definitionFit: Nicked is British slang for stolen as well as for arrested, so the two words are synonyms.
